significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish both a behavioral phenomenon—"hearsay-marked premise[s] given in Turkish" reduce certainty or alter English answers—and a causal mechanism in which a compact "information-source" direction controls certainty and cross-language leakage; the asserted dependence of coupling strength on evidential obligatoriness makes this a form-(iii) predictive relation, not merely an existence claim. It would predict stronger certainty shifts in grammatically evidential languages and source-conditioned behavior after language switching, constraining interpretations of shared multilingual computation relevant to work such as Wendler et al. (2024) on English-centric latent processing. Verified false outcomes are also distinguishable and informative: absent encoding would imply models ignore this grammatical distinction, while encoding without leakage would support compartmentalization, although a blanket null would not rule out every alternative representation. After substituting the claim with the generic topic, I would not retain this score: the specific obligatoriness-to-certainty relation and Turkish-to-English causal contamination are materially sharper than the median shared-versus-language-specific representation hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "information-source direction," the relationship between "evidential obligatoriness" and certainty shift, and an intervention that can "ablate the direction to remove cross-lingual leakage." Reading the direction after a premise but before generation could provide ex-ante lead time to flag or suppress source-induced answer changes, though its clearest immediate users would be multilingual-model researchers and auditors rather than general deployers. After per-model re-extraction, the direction itself must be rediscovered, but the claimed relation predicts that obligatory evidential marking will produce stronger certainty coupling and that source state will persist across language switches; its asserted scope spans multilingual LLMs and multiple language classes rather than one fixed dataset. The topic-substitution check lowers no further: generic cross-language transfer supplies neither this source-sensitive diagnostic nor the predicted obligatoriness gradient, but the absence of a fully stated deployment rule keeps the reach below the highest bands.
